topic: State breach notification and data security

notes.front: What is a breach of the security of the system under Nevada's breach law?
notes.back: Unauthorised acquisition of computerised data that materially compromises the security, confidentiality or integrity of personal information the data collector holds.
notes.explanation: A good-faith acquisition by an employee or agent for a legitimate purpose is not a breach, if the data is not misused or further disclosed.
notes.example: Like a burglar taking copies of your client files, as opposed to a clerk opening them to do her job.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.020
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
introduces: breach of the security of the system
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: What is the encryption safe harbour in state breach notification laws?
notes.back: The rule that notice duties attach to unencrypted personal information, so the acquisition of properly encrypted data does not trigger them.
notes.explanation: Nevada requires notice to residents whose unencrypted personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired.
notes.example: Like losing a locked safe without its key: the box is gone, but what is inside stays unreadable.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.220(1) and 603A.040
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: What is credit monitoring?
notes.back: A service that tells a consumer about material additions or modifications to their file at a consumer reporting agency.
notes.explanation: Federal law requires nationwide consumer reporting agencies to offer a free electronic version to active duty military consumers.
notes.example: Like a doorbell camera on your credit file: it alerts you when someone new comes calling.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. 1681c-1(k) (credit monitoring for active duty military consumers)
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: shall provide a free electronic credit monitoring service that, at a minimum, notifies a consumer of material additions or modifications to the file of the consumer at the consumer reporting agency to any consumer who provides to the consumer reporting agency— (A) appropriate proof that the consumer is an active duty military consumer

notes.front: Under Nevada's breach law, what are two data elements that make a person's name 'personal information'?
notes.back: Any two of: social security number; driver's licence or identification card number; card or account number with access code; health insurance identification number, among others.
notes.explanation: Each element counts only in combination with the first name or initial and last name, and only when not encrypted.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.040(1)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: Can online log-in details alone be personal information under Nevada's breach law?
notes.back: Yes, with a name: a user name, unique identifier or email address together with a password or security answer that gives account access.
notes.explanation: It is listed alongside identity numbers, card numbers and health insurance numbers.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.040(1)(e)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: A breach at a Nevada insurer exposes unencrypted files listing customers' full names with their health insurance identification numbers. Is this personal information under Nevada's breach law?
notes.back: D: Yes: a name combined with a health insurance identification number, unencrypted, is personal information.
notes.choices:
A) No, only social security numbers count
B) No, because insurers are exempt
C) Only if the files also held addresses
D) Yes, name plus health insurance number
notes.choicesExplained: A: the list has several elements. B: the definition has no insurer exemption. C: addresses are not needed.
notes.explanation: A medical or health insurance identification number is one of the listed data elements.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.040(1)(d)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: A hospital billing clerk in Nevada opens patient account records to process a refund, as her job requires, and uses them for nothing else. Is this a breach of the security of the system?
notes.back: B: No: good-faith acquisition by an employee for a legitimate purpose is excluded.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, any access to personal information is a breach
B) No, good-faith acquisition by an employee is excluded
C) Yes, unless the data was encrypted
D) Only if more than 500 people are affected
notes.choicesExplained: A: the definition requires unauthorised acquisition. C: encryption is irrelevant when access is authorised. D: numbers affect notice, not the definition.
notes.explanation: The exclusion holds while the information is not used for an unrelated purpose or disclosed further.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.020
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: A laptop holding customers' names and social security numbers is stolen in Nevada. The disk was encrypted to a recognised standard and the key was not taken. Must customers be notified under Nevada law?
notes.back: D: No: notice is owed for unencrypted personal information, and the data here was encrypted.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, every theft must be notified
B) Yes, but only to the attorney general
C) Only if the laptop is not recovered in 30 days
D) No, the encryption safe harbour applies
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the duty attaches to unencrypted information. C: there is no recovery period in the law.
notes.explanation: Nevada's definition of personal information covers names and data elements that are not encrypted.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.040 and 603A.220
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: What counts as encryption for Nevada's security and breach law?
notes.back: Protecting stored or moving data with technology adopted by an established standards body, making it unreadable without the keys.
notes.explanation: The Federal Information Processing Standards of the National Institute of Standards and Technology are given as an example.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.215(5)(b)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When must a Nevada data collector notify residents of a breach?
notes.back: In the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.
notes.explanation: Timing may reflect law enforcement's legitimate needs and measures to find the breach's scope and restore system integrity.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.220(1)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: When may a breach notice be delayed under Nevada's breach law?
notes.back: When a law enforcement agency decides notice would impede a criminal investigation; notice follows once it will not compromise it.
notes.explanation: The delay depends on the agency's determination, not the data collector's own view.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.220(3)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: What are the three ways a Nevada data collector may give breach notice?
notes.back: Written notice, electronic notice consistent with the federal Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act, or substitute notice in listed circumstances.
notes.explanation: Substitute notice is for high cost, very large numbers, or missing contact details.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.220(4)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: When may a Nevada data collector use substitute breach notice?
notes.back: When notice would cost over 250,000 dollars, more than 500,000 people are affected, or it lacks enough contact information.
notes.explanation: Substitute notice combines email where possible, a conspicuous website posting and notice to major statewide media.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.220(4)(c)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: If a Nevada data collector must notify more than {{c1::1,000}} persons at any one time, it must also tell the nationwide consumer reporting agencies when and what it notified.
notes.explanation: Nevada ties this extra step to the size of the notification.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.220(6)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: Police ask a Nevada retailer to hold off notifying customers of a breach because notice would impede their criminal investigation. What should the retailer do?
notes.back: A: Delay notice until the police determine it will not compromise the investigation, then notify.
notes.choices:
A) Delay until police say notice will not compromise the investigation
B) Notify at once regardless
C) Never notify, as police are involved
D) Notify only the attorney general
notes.choicesExplained: B: the law allows the delay. C: notice is delayed, not cancelled. D: the law does not substitute an AG notice.
notes.explanation: Nevada allows delay only on the law enforcement agency's determination.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.220(3)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: Whom must a business notify of a breach under California's breach law, as the Attorney General describes it?
notes.back: Any California resident whose unencrypted personal information was, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired by an unauthorised person.
notes.explanation: State agencies have the same duty under a parallel section of the Civil Code.
notes.source: California Attorney General, Data Security Breach Reporting
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: When must a business send the California Attorney General a copy of its breach notice?
notes.back: When it must notify more than 500 California residents of a single breach: one sample copy, without personal information, submitted electronically.
notes.explanation: The Attorney General publishes submitted breach notices in an online search.
notes.source: California Attorney General, Data Security Breach Reporting
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: A company must notify 800 California residents of one breach. What must it also do?
notes.back: C: Submit one sample copy of the notice, without personal information, electronically to the California Attorney General.
notes.choices:
A) Notify the CPPA within 72 hours
B) Publish the notice in a newspaper
C) Send a sample copy to the Attorney General
D) Nothing more
notes.choicesExplained: A: the duty runs to the Attorney General, and there is no 72-hour rule here. B: not required by this rule. D: over 500 residents triggers the extra step.
notes.explanation: More than 500 residents from a single breach triggers the sample-copy duty.
notes.source: California Attorney General, Data Security Breach Reporting
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: After a breach, a company's prompt good-faith investigation finds that misuse of Utah residents' personal information for identity theft or fraud is not reasonably likely. Must it notify them under Utah law?
notes.back: B: No: Utah requires notice when the investigation shows misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, every breach must be notified
B) No, misuse is not reasonably likely
C) Yes, but only to the Utah Cyber Center
D) Only if more than 1,000 residents are affected
notes.choicesExplained: A: Utah's trigger is a finding of actual or likely misuse. C: official notices come on top of, not instead of, resident notice. D: numbers add recipients but do not create the trigger.
notes.explanation: Utah's law starts with a reasonable, prompt investigation into the likelihood of misuse for identity theft or fraud.
notes.source: Utah S.B. 127 (2023 General Session), Cybersecurity Amendments, enrolled copy, § 13-44-202, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Whom did Utah's S.B. 127 (2023) add to breach notices affecting 500 or more Utah residents?
notes.back: The Office of the Attorney General and the Utah Cyber Center.
notes.explanation: At 1,000 or more residents, the nationwide consumer reporting agencies must also be told.
notes.source: Utah S.B. 127 (2023 General Session), Cybersecurity Amendments, enrolled copy, § 13-44-202, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company finds that misuse for identity theft is reasonably likely after a breach affecting 600 Utah residents. Under Utah law as amended in 2023, whom must it notify?
notes.back: B: Each affected resident, the Office of the Attorney General and the Utah Cyber Center.
notes.choices:
A) Only the affected residents
B) The residents, the Attorney General and the Utah Cyber Center
C) The residents and the consumer reporting agencies only
D) Only the Utah Cyber Center
notes.choicesExplained: A: 500 or more residents adds official notices. C: consumer reporting agencies are required at 1,000. D: residents must be notified too.
notes.explanation: At 500 or more residents, the Attorney General and the Cyber Center are added; consumer reporting agencies come in at 1,000.
notes.source: Utah S.B. 127 (2023 General Session), Cybersecurity Amendments, enrolled copy, § 13-44-202, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do Nevada and Utah differ in what triggers individual breach notice?
notes.back: Nevada: acquisition, or reasonable belief of acquisition, of unencrypted personal information; Utah: an investigation finding misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely.
notes.explanation: Utah builds a risk-of-misuse test into the trigger; Nevada's turns on acquisition.
notes.source: Utah S.B. 127 (2023 General Session), Cybersecurity Amendments, enrolled copy, § 13-44-202, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: How do California and Utah compare on notifying state officials of a breach?
notes.back: Both use a 500-resident line: California wants a sample notice to the Attorney General; Utah wants notice to the Attorney General and Utah Cyber Center.
notes.explanation: California's line is more than 500 residents; Utah's is 500 or more.
notes.source: California Attorney General, Data Security Breach Reporting
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: What security duty does Nevada impose on a data collector keeping records of residents' personal information?
notes.back: To implement and maintain reasonable security measures against unauthorised access, acquisition, destruction, use, modification or disclosure.
notes.explanation: Contracts disclosing such information must require the recipient to do the same.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.210(1) and (3)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Nevada data collector that does not take payment cards ships a backup drive of customer personal information to an outside storage site beyond its control. What does Nevada law require?
notes.back: D: Encryption of the information on the drive.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, if the courier is trusted
B) PCI DSS certification of the storage site
C) A signed receipt from the site
D) Encryption of the information
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: trust and receipts do not replace encryption. B: PCI DSS applies to collectors that accept payment cards.
notes.explanation: Collectors outside the payment card rule must encrypt data storage devices moved beyond their logical or physical controls.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.215(2)(b)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
uses: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

notes.front: A Nevada company hands customer records to a marketing agency under a contract silent on security. What does Nevada law say about that contract?
notes.back: A: It must require the agency to implement and maintain reasonable security measures to protect the records.
notes.choices:
A) It must require reasonable security measures
B) It is fine, because security is the agency's own business
C) It needs approval from the attorney general
D) It must be registered with the state
notes.choicesExplained: B: the law requires the contract to impose security duties. C and D: no approval or registration is required.
notes.explanation: Nevada extends its reasonable-security duty to recipients through the contract.
notes.source: Nevada Revised Statutes chapter 603A, NRS 603A.210(3)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who may bring a civil action under the CCPA's data breach section?
notes.back: A consumer whose nonencrypted, nonredacted personal information, or email plus password, is accessed and taken, stolen or disclosed because the business lacked reasonable security.
notes.explanation: Only nonencrypted and nonredacted data, or account log-in data, can found the claim.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.150(a)(1), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: Any consumer whose nonencrypted and nonredacted personal information, as defined in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) of Section 1798.81.5, or whose email address in combination with a password or security question and answer that would permit access to the account is subject to an unauthorized access and exfiltration, theft, or disclosure

notes.front: What statutory damages range applies per consumer per incident under the CCPA's breach action from 1 January 2025?
notes.back: 107 to 799 dollars, or actual damages if greater.
notes.explanation: The range was 100 to 750 dollars before the inflation adjustment.
notes.source: CPPA, Updated Monetary Thresholds in CCPA (effective 1 Jan. 2025)
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: Monetary damages range per consumer per incident Not less than $107 and not greater than $799 per consumer per incident or actual damages, whichever is greater. Not less than $100 and not greater than $750

notes.front: What must a consumer do before suing a business for statutory damages under the CCPA breach section?
notes.back: Give the business 30 days' written notice identifying the provisions allegedly violated.
notes.explanation: If the business actually cures within those 30 days and gives a written statement, no statutory damages action may follow.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.150(b), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: a consumer provides a business 30 days’ written notice identifying the specific provisions of this title the consumer alleges have been or are being violated. In the event a cure is possible, if within the 30 days the business actually cures the noticed violation and provides the consumer an express written statement that the violations have been cured

notes.front: Does putting reasonable security in place after a breach count as a cure under the CCPA breach section?
notes.back: No. Implementing and maintaining reasonable security after a breach is not a cure for that breach.
notes.explanation: A cure after the breach cannot come from simply fixing security going forward.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.150(b), p. 46
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: The implementation and maintenance of reasonable security procedures and practices pursuant to Section 1798.81.5 following a breach does not constitute a cure with respect to that breach.

notes.front: Can a consumer use the CCPA's breach action to sue over other CCPA violations, such as ignoring an opt-out?
notes.back: No. The action applies only to the security breaches defined in section 1798.150 and cannot rest on other sections.
notes.explanation: The CCPA also says nothing in it is the basis for a private right of action under any other law.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), CPPA text effective 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.150(c), p. 47
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: The cause of action established by this section shall apply only to violations as defined in subdivision (a) and shall not be based on violations of any other section of this title. Nothing in this title shall be interpreted to serve as the basis for a private right of action under any other law.

notes.front: Hackers steal unencrypted customer records from a California retailer that ignored basic security. Two hundred customers sue for statutory damages. Under the CCPA from 2025, what can each recover?
notes.back: C: Between 107 and 799 dollars per incident, or actual damages if greater, after giving 30 days' notice.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: only the CPPA can act
B) Up to 7,988 dollars each
C) 107 to 799 dollars each, or actual damages if greater
D) Unlimited punitive damages
notes.choicesExplained: A: the breach section gives consumers a private right of action. B: that is the administrative fine ceiling. D: the statute sets a statutory range.
notes.explanation: The breach section allows statutory damages per consumer per incident within the adjusted range.
notes.source: CPPA, Updated Monetary Thresholds in CCPA (effective 1 Jan. 2025)
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (California state website conditions of use)
notes.evidence: Not less than $107 and not greater than $799 per consumer per incident or actual damages, whichever is greater.

notes.front: How does HIPAA's breach notice deadline differ from Nevada's?
notes.back: HIPAA: without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery; Nevada: most expedient time possible, with no fixed maximum.
notes.explanation: HIPAA adds an outer limit in days to the 'without unreasonable delay' standard.
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.
uses: breach of the security of the system

notes.front: How can credit monitoring feature in a breach notice under the FTC's Health Breach Notification Rule?
notes.back: As an example of what the entity is doing to protect affected individuals, which the notice must describe.
notes.explanation: The notice must briefly describe investigation, mitigation and protective steps, such as offering credit monitoring.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 318 (Health Breach Notification Rule), 2026 edition, § 318.6, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US Government work)
notes.evidence: to protect against any further breaches, and to protect affected individuals, such as offering credit monitoring or other services
